questions.stem: After executing a `lookup_order` call, the developer's loop sends the next API request with only the model's previous assistant message appended. The model then calls `lookup_order` again with identical arguments, and repeats this several times. What is wrong?

options.text: The loop never appends a `tool_result` block, with the matching `tool_use_id`, in a user message, so the model never sees the output.
options.why: Every tool call's result must go back into the conversation history.

options.text: The model needs `tool_choice: {"type": "none"}` after the first call, to stop it from requesting the same tool repeatedly.
options.why: This would block all further tool use instead of supplying the missing result.

options.text: `lookup_order` lacks an idempotency key, so the model can't tell that its earlier call has already completed.
options.why: Idempotency protects side effects. It doesn't deliver results to the model.

options.text: The system prompt should forbid repeating a tool call with identical arguments within the same conversation.
options.why: This treats the symptom. The model is repeating the call because it lacks the result.

questions.explanation: An agentic loop executes the requested tools, appends the `tool_result` blocks to history, and calls the model again. Missing results cause repeated or hallucinated calls.

questions.stem: Larkspur's support playbook contains many rules. Which TWO of them should be enforced programmatically rather than through prompt instructions? (Select TWO.)

options.text: No refund may be processed until `get_customer` has returned a verified identity for that customer.
options.why: This is a hard compliance rule that must hold every time, so it needs a programmatic gate.

options.text: Refunds above $500 require explicit approval from a human on the Tier-2 team before they are issued.
options.why: This is a financial control to enforce deterministically, for example with an interception hook.

options.text: Mention the loyalty programme to customers who have placed three or more orders in the past year.
options.why: This is a soft behaviour where occasional misses are harmless, so a prompt suits it.

options.text: Keep responses friendly, concise and free of internal jargon, such as warehouse codes or system names.
options.why: Tone and style guidance is exactly what prompts handle well.

options.text: Apologise once, not repeatedly, when an order has been delayed by more than five business days.
options.why: This is a conversational nuance that is better shaped by prompts and examples.

questions.explanation: Use code (hooks, prerequisite gates) for rules with compliance or financial consequences. Use prompts for style and soft guidance.

questions.stem: A PreToolUse hook blocks `process_refund` for customers who haven't been verified. When it blocks a call, what should the hook return to the agent?

options.text: An empty response, so the agent treats the refund as not having happened and moves on without confusing the customer.
options.why: Silent failure leaves the agent unsure what happened. It may tell the customer a refund was issued.

options.text: A success response carrying a hidden flag, so the customer sees a smooth experience while the refund is queued for review.
options.why: Masking a block as success misleads both the agent and the customer.

options.text: A structured reason, such as "blocked: customer not verified; call get_customer first", so the agent can recover.
options.why: An informative denial lets the agent self-correct within the conversation.

options.text: An exception that ends the session, so blocked refund attempts are always investigated by the security team.
options.why: This is disproportionate for a recoverable ordering mistake.

questions.explanation: Interception hooks should block deterministically and explain why, so that the agent can redirect, for example to verification or escalation.

questions.stem: A team proposes replacing the agent with a fixed decision tree: if the message mentions "refund", ask for the order ID, then look it up, then refund. Why is the agentic design generally preferred here, and where does deterministic logic still belong?

options.text: Decision trees are always safer because they are deterministic, so the agent should be replaced entirely for refunds.
options.why: Rigid trees fail on varied, multi-concern conversations and hurt resolution rates.

options.text: Messages vary too much for fixed trees, so the model picks next steps from tool results. Code still enforces policy boundaries.
options.why: Model-driven flow plus programmatic guardrails is the intended hybrid.

options.text: The agent should handle everything, including policy enforcement, since modern models follow instructions reliably enough.
options.why: Critical rules need deterministic enforcement.

options.text: Use the tree for refunds and the agent for everything else, so each part uses its strengths without overlap.
options.why: Refund conversations are often the most varied ones, so splitting this way loses the agent's value where it matters most.

questions.explanation: Agentic loops let the model decide which tool to call next, rather than following a fixed tree, while hooks and gates enforce the non-negotiable rules.

questions.stem: The agent sometimes answers order-status questions from memory without calling `lookup_order`. A developer fixes this by setting `tool_choice: {"type": "any"}` on every request. What side effect should you expect?

options.text: None. `any` only forces a tool call when one of the tools is relevant to the customer's message.
options.why: That describes `auto`.

options.text: It forces `lookup_order` on every turn, because it is the most frequently used tool in the conversation history.
options.why: Forcing one specific tool requires the named-tool form.

options.text: It disables parallel tool calls, so conversations that need several lookups become noticeably slower.
options.why: That isn't what `any` does.

options.text: The model must call a tool on every turn and can never reply in plain text. Better descriptions and instructions are the right fix.
options.why: `any` forces a tool call on every turn.

questions.explanation: `auto`: the model decides. `any`: it must call some tool. A named tool: it must call that tool. Forcing tool use globally prevents text replies.

questions.stem: A customer asks for a refund on a custom-engraved watch delivered 10 days ago, citing a typo in the engraving. The refund policy covers damaged and late items but doesn't mention personalised goods or engraving errors. What should the agent do?

options.text: Apply the standard 30-day refund policy, since the item was delivered recently and nothing in the policy forbids it.
options.why: This improvises policy for a case the policy doesn't address.

options.text: Deny the refund politely, since personalised goods aren't listed as eligible, and offer a discount code instead.
options.why: This also improvises, and it may wrongly deny a legitimate claim.

options.text: Treat it as a policy gap: tell the customer it needs review, and escalate with a structured summary.
options.why: Policy gaps and exceptions are escalation triggers.

options.text: Ask the customer to upload a photo of the engraving, decide whether the typo is the company's fault, and refund if so.
options.why: Gathering evidence is reasonable, but the agent still has no policy basis for the decision.

questions.explanation: Escalate when a case falls outside the documented policy, rather than inventing policy.

questions.stem: Two search subagents are assigned "EV charging pricing" and "EV charging business models". They return heavily overlapping sources and findings, which uses about 40% of the budget twice. What should the coordinator do differently?

options.text: Let both run as-is, and have the synthesis agent deduplicate overlapping findings before writing the brief.
options.why: The budget is already spent by then. This treats the symptom.

options.text: Partition scope explicitly when delegating: give each subagent distinct boundaries and exclusions so the work doesn't overlap.
options.why: Explicit scope partitioning avoids duplicated work.

options.text: Merge the two subtopics into a single subagent task, so one agent covers both without repeating any searches.
options.why: This loses parallelism and focus on two genuinely different questions.

options.text: Cap each subagent at five search results, so that any overlap between them is limited to a few shared sources.
options.why: They would still overlap, just with less data.

questions.explanation: The coordinator should partition subagent scopes to avoid duplication and gaps.

questions.stem: Clients report that some sections of their briefs are thin, typically one paragraph with a single source, while others are rich. The coordinator currently delegates once and then hands everything to synthesis. Which change best improves completeness?

options.text: Run every subagent twice with slightly different prompts, and merge both outputs to increase coverage.
options.why: This duplicates work blindly instead of targeting the gaps.

options.text: Instruct the report agent to expand thin sections using general knowledge, clearly marked as background context.
options.why: Padding without evidence lowers quality and weakens the citation guarantees.

options.text: Raise each subagent's search result limit, so every section starts with more raw material from the beginning.
options.why: More results everywhere costs more and doesn't specifically address which sections are thin.

options.text: Add a refinement loop: the coordinator checks coverage against the quality criteria and re-delegates targeted follow-ups for gaps.
options.why: The coordinator evaluates, finds gaps and re-delegates.

questions.explanation: Coordinators can run iterative refinement loops: evaluate output against the criteria, then delegate follow-ups.

questions.stem: The team wants a reusable "fact-checker" subagent with its own instructions, a restricted toolset (fetch only, no search), and a clear description so the coordinator knows when to use it. How should it be defined in the Agent SDK?

options.text: As an `AgentDefinition` with a description, a system prompt and a restricted tools list.
options.why: This is how the SDK defines specialised subagents.

options.text: As a paragraph in the coordinator's system prompt that tells it to adopt a fact-checker persona when verifying claims.
options.why: This gives no isolated context and no tool restriction.

options.text: As a separate MCP server that exposes a `fact_check` tool, which internally calls the model with fetch access.
options.why: This is possible but heavyweight. MCP servers expose tools, not agent definitions.

options.text: As a project skill in `.claude/skills/fact-checker/` with `allowed-tools: WebFetch` in its SKILL.md frontmatter.
options.why: Skills are Claude Code assets, not how an Agent SDK coordinator defines subagents.

questions.explanation: `AgentDefinition` provides the description, system prompt and tool restrictions for subagents.

questions.stem: A client orders a recurring monthly brief with the same fixed structure: market size, top five players, regulatory changes and outlook. The sources are largely the same each month. Which workflow design fits best?

options.text: Fully adaptive decomposition each month, so the coordinator can discover new angles the fixed structure might miss.
options.why: Adaptive decomposition adds variability that a fixed, agreed structure doesn't need.

options.text: A single long prompt that writes the whole brief from the sources, since the structure is simple and familiar.
options.why: This loses focus, per-section validation and citation tracking.

options.text: A prompt chain or fixed pipeline with one stage per section, since the structure is stable and predictable.
options.why: Predictable, repeatable structures suit chaining.

options.text: Reuse last month's brief and ask the report agent to update only the figures it detects as changed.
options.why: This risks carrying stale claims forward and misses new developments.

questions.explanation: Use fixed chaining for known structures and adaptive decomposition for open-ended discovery.

questions.stem: The synthesis agent receives prose summaries from the subagents and often can't tell which document or page each claim came from. Which TWO changes to the subagents' outputs help most? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Return findings as structured records: claim, evidence excerpt, source ID or URL, and page or section.
options.why: Structured content preserves attribution across hops.

options.text: Attach metadata such as publication date and source type (regulator, analyst, press) to each finding.
options.why: Metadata supports provenance and recency judgements.

options.text: Return longer, more detailed prose summaries, so that more context about each source is preserved.
options.why: Length doesn't fix attribution.

options.text: Strip source references from subagent outputs to save tokens, and let synthesis re-derive them from the raw documents.
options.why: This destroys provenance and duplicates work.

options.text: Have each subagent write its section directly into the final report, so citations never pass through synthesis.
options.why: This bypasses the coordinator and synthesis, and fragments the report.

questions.explanation: Pass structured content plus metadata between agents to preserve attribution.

questions.stem: The coordinator's context grows past 150k tokens on large briefs, because each subagent returns the full text of every page it fetched. Coordination quality drops noticeably in the later steps. What is the best fix?

options.text: Move the coordinator to a model with a larger context window, so all the fetched content fits without truncation.
options.why: Attention still dilutes over the extra content, and costs rise.

options.text: Have subagents return concise, structured findings with source references instead of raw pages.
options.why: Subagents exist partly to absorb verbose work and return distilled results.

options.text: Have the coordinator summarise each subagent's raw output as it arrives, and keep only its own summaries in history.
options.why: The bloat still enters the coordinator's context first, and its summaries are lossy.

options.text: Limit each subagent to a single search query, so fewer pages are fetched and returned per subtask.
options.why: This hurts research quality instead of fixing what is returned.

questions.explanation: Keep the coordinator's context lean: subagents return structured summaries with metadata, not raw dumps.

questions.stem: The `web_fetch` tool returns HTTP 403 for paywalled news sites. The search subagent keeps retrying those URLs, sometimes five times each, before giving up. How should the tool report this condition?

options.text: As an empty page with a success status, so the agent concludes there is nothing useful at that URL and moves on.
options.why: This masks an access failure as an empty result.

options.text: As a transient error, so the agent waits and retries later in case the paywall was a temporary glitch.
options.why: This is the wrong category, and it wastes calls on a permanent condition.

options.text: As a permission or access error with `isRetryable: false`, so the agent moves to other sources.
options.why: Categorised, non-retryable errors stop futile retries.

options.text: As an exception that ends the subagent's task, so the coordinator can reassign the topic to another subagent.
options.why: This is disproportionate. One blocked URL shouldn't kill the subtask.

questions.explanation: Error categories plus retryability guide the agent's recovery: retry only transient failures.
